title: Static and Global State Across Calls
quickIdea: A static local is one object shared by every call of the function, so a recursive function can see the writes of its own earlier calls - and on the way back up it sees the final value, not the value it started with.
remember: A static local is initialised once, before the first call, and keeps its value between calls and across the recursion. An auto local is a fresh object in every frame.

GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.35: count(3) with static int d = 1 prints 3 1 2 2 1 3 4 4 4. The descent prints n and d for n = 3, 2, 1, and the three 4s come from the unwinding, where every frame reads the same final d.
A global variable behaves the same way for this purpose: one object, visible to every frame, so a global counter counts all the calls rather than the calls of one frame.
Because the shared object is written on the descent, a read on the unwinding sees the last value written, not the value at the time that frame was created.
Make d an auto local and the same program prints 3 1 2 1 1 1 2 2 2 - the value each frame would have had if it owned its own copy, which is one of the paper's options.
The alternative design is to pass the accumulator as a parameter or to return it; then every frame is independent and the output order becomes the only thing that differs.

example.prompt: void count(int n) { static int d = 1; printf("%d", n); printf("%d", d); d++; if (n > 1) count(n-1); printf("%d", d); } What does count(3) print?
example.work: count(3) prints 3 and 1, then d becomes 2, then calls count(2), which prints 2 and 2 and raises d to 3, then count(1) prints 1 and 3 and raises d to 4 and returns after printing 4. The two outer frames then each print the same d, now 4.

gateAngle: This is the standard way GATE combines recursion with storage duration: the recursion supplies the order, the static variable supplies the shared value. Both wrong answers in 2016 Set 1 Q.35 come from treating d as an auto local.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.35: what does count(3) print?
variations.why: The static d is one object; the unwinding reads its final value three times.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: What would the same program print if d were declared auto instead of static?
variations.why: Each frame now has its own d, which is 1 on entry and 2 after the increment, so every unwinding print is 2.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does count(4) end with four 5s rather than one?
variations.answer: Because d is incremented on every activation: four activations raise it from 1 to 5, and each of the four frames prints the same shared object after its call returns. The full output is 4 1 3 2 2 3 1 4 5 5 5 5.
variations.why: The number of trailing repeats equals the number of activations that reach the print after the call, which is the depth of the recursion.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A global counter is incremented at the top of a recursive function. What does it hold when the call returns?
variations.answer: The total number of activations, including the base-case ones, because every frame increments the same object.
variations.why: This is the cheapest way to answer 'how many calls' in practice, and it is why the recurrence and the counter agree.

trap.what: Assuming each frame owns a copy of a static local.
trap.why: static changes the storage duration, not the scope. The name is still local to the function, but the object is created once and shared by every call, so a write in one frame is visible in all the others.
trap.counterexample: In count(3) the three trailing 4s are impossible if each frame had its own d: they are the same object read three times.

check.question: void f(int n) { static int c = 0; c++; if (n > 1) f(n-1); printf("%d", c); } What does f(3) print?
check.explanation: Three activations raise the shared c to 3 before any of them prints; all three then print the same object, which holds 3.

visual.title: Recursion
covers: a recursive definition: smaller copy plus a base case
one frame per call: own parameters, own locals, own return address
nothing is computed on the way down; values combine on the way up
fact(n) and sumTo(n): calls = depth = n+1
the C standard does not require tail call optimisation
static local inside a recursion is one object shared by all frames
GATE 2011 foo(n, r) is the base-r digit sum; foo(513,2) = 2
T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 gives n+1 calls; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives n log2 n + n
